posts.content_md:
Hi all!

I've made a computer program that makes holograms from a given digital 3D model.

One of the input variables for the program is the frequency of the object beam and reference beam (which are always the same in my case).

Though the width of the [square] hologram screen (in 3D space) is always 100 units, the number of pixels in the output hologram is a user-defined variable.

My question is:

How many pixels across will my hologram have to be in order for it to sufficiently store the interference patterns of the hologram. When I first started this project, I did not take into account the enormous detail level of the interference patterns of a hologram.

I'm thinking that the distance between pixels will have to be less than the period of the object/reference beams (which is very small). In my case, since I'm using virtual coherent light with a frequency of 5^15Hz, the pixels will have to be at or less than 5^-15 units apart. This means that, given the width of the hologram screen and the number of pixels, the distance between pixels can be found using the following formula:

distance=width/# of pixels

If d is, in fact, supposed to be less than or equal to the period of the given light, then:

period>width/# of pixels or frequency<# of pixels/width

Because I am limited by CPU ability, this means that I am either going to have to use very small hologram widths, or I am going to have to use lower frequencies for my virtual coherent light beams.

So, I guess my next question is:

If I use frequencies in my program that are smaller than that of visible light, how can I modify the output hologram so that it will be compatible with a reconstruction beam of a larger frequency?

Finally, onto what medium should I print the output holograms from my program, and should I try for reflection or transmission holograms? I take it is not as simple as printing out the hologram to a regular sheet of printer paper. (sorry, but I know basically nothing about hologram medium materials)

Also, I understand that a transmission hologram works via diffraction of the reference beam, but I am unsure how a reference beam interacts with a reflection holograms in order to reveal the 3D image.

Sorry for the rag-tag presentation of questions; if some of my questions are not clear, please ask me to elaborate.

Thank you very much!

Andy

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Andy, welcome to the forum. I have never made a CGH, but have seen several very good ones made by alumni of the MIT (former) Spatial Imaging Group. There are several ways to proceed making them on your own. You are correct about laser printers lacking the resolution needed for a good CGH, although some people have reported success there. In general, you want 1000-2000 dots per millimeter in the holographic substrate.

One trick you can use is to print it out (at whatever resolution you can), and then photograph it. You can shine a laser through the film negative. However, I don't know what type of film to recommend with enough resolution to result in any sort of decent reconstruction. (One drawback of having poor resolution is that the reconstruction angle will be very narrow. That is, you won't have any "look-around" (motion parallax). You'll simply reconstruct what looks like a 2-D image.)

You can also make a multiplex hologram by depicting the scene from a variety of viewpoints computationally, and then doing a "rainbow" hologram. For some ideas on this, see the papers and theses by Michael Halle [here,](http://www.media.mit.edu/spi/spiPubs.htm) such as "the generalized holographic stereogram." You can record a multiperspective hologram onto holographic film in a series of steps.

Maybe I didn't answer your question. The accuracy of your computer physics modeling can probably be bounded by the resolution of your real-world holographic substrate.

g

If you want to solve the problem for a larger hologram take a look at the hardware accelleration in a video card. MIT is reporting that there are algorythms there that speed up the process greatly. I have run a couple with the software liked in my first post. It is not as slow as I thought but it also does not have an off axis reference. The code for an off axis refference would slow things down considerably. 

If you really just made a phisical model and did a ray tracing of all the light there is a much faster computational method. 

This is a good book to understand the basic math:

Optical Holography: Principles, Techniques and Applications (Cambridge Studies in Modern Optics) (Paperback) 

But to reduce this math computationally you will need to study Fourier Transforms and especially the FFT. An intrductory book on signal processing theory would be good as well.

[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform)

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
**Amplitude versus intensity**

Hmm. I suspect that he might have plotted electric field amplitude rather than the irradiance, which is proportional to the time average of the *square* of the electric field amplitude. That is, according to Benton's course notes, if

E(*x, y, t*) = *A* sin (2 pi *nu t*) V/m,

then its average squared value will be

*A*^2 / 2,

and it will deliver an irradiance of

I(x,y) = (epsilon-naught c) < | E(x,y,t) |^2 >time avg = (epsilon-naught *c / 2) A^2

= 2.65 x 10^(-3) E^2(rms) W/m^2 

in MKS.

**Fringe Applet**

I think you (and others here) may find this Media Lab demonstration of fringes very interesting. [(here)](http://courses.media.mit.edu/2002spring/mas450/holodemos/index.html). Oh, wait, they're not available at that URL anymore! Perhaps someone can find them by Googling.

-g

My program uses the following to calculate the intensity of a single pixel on the hologram screen:

screen[y][x]=sin((2*pi*hz*dist(bloc,pc[y][x])));

where:

- screen represents the z value of a pixel on the screen at the coordinate (x, y, 0).

- hz is the input frequency

- dist(bloc, pc[y][x]) returns the distance between the beam origin and the location of the pixel being calculated.

Andy,

Yes, you could use superimposed zone plates (with "focal lengths" and centerpoints of your choosing) as one way to create a simple hologram. However, I believe the drawback will be that you'll only be able to depict scenes that are translucent. (I.e., there will be no occlusion.)

Anyhow, keep experimenting, and keep in mind that irradiance is different than instantaneous electric field strength.
